extracted.intended_audience: comedy writers, stand-up comedians, and humorists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for constructing short jokes or humorous lines that use the 'rule of three' — list three elements where the first two set up a pattern and the third breaks it for comedic effect. Useful for one-liners, punchlines, and short comedic beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exactly three items
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there exactly three items in the list?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule specifies listing three things; three is the smallest number that both creates a pattern and allows it to be broken. Check for too few (no pattern) or too many (dilutes rhythm). Example positive: 'I love beaches, sunsets, and crippling debt.' Anti-pattern: longer lists that lose punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: First two establish a clear, expected pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the first two items establish a clear, expected pattern?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first two elements should set up a recognizable pattern or expectation (parallelism, similar semantic class, tone). This builds tension and primes the audience for the twist. Example: two mundane or sincere items that create an expectation of a third similar item.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third item subverts the pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the third item subvert that pattern?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comedic effect depends on the third item breaking the pattern established by the first two (incongruity, absurdity, surprise). A straight parallel third (e.g., 'Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness') is not subversive; the joke version must invert or mismatch expectations to create humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third item is placed last (anchored at end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the third item placed last (anchored at end)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the punch-line element at the end to maximize its impact; anchoring the subversion as the final element intensifies the release of tension. Example: after a polite or long-winding intro, the abrupt or crude final line lands stronger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third item is maximally surprising or absurd given the setup
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the third item maximally surprising or absurd given the setup?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The third item should escalate the incongruity relative to the setup — be as unexpected and exaggerated as the context allows while remaining coherent enough to be understood. Avoid predictable or weak third items that only mildly diverge from the pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third item should be the funniest of the three
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the third item the funniest of the three?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The third element frequently functions as the punch line and should carry the most humor. Evaluate whether the emotional/comedic payoff is concentrated in the third item rather than earlier elements. If earlier items steal laughs, the structure may be weakened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and rhythm (use three for concision and pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the construction use the smallest amount of information needed to create a pattern and rhythm (brevity)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three combines brevity and rhythm: it's the minimal set that forms a pattern yet allows a break. Prefer concise wording and a rhythmic cadence so the pattern and the break are obvious and sharp. Excess verbiage or complex embedding can blunt the punch.
